content: Methyl salicylate, also known as salicylic acid methyl ester, oil of wintergreen, betula oil, or methyl-2-hydroxybenzoate, is a chemical compound with the formula C6H4(HO)COOCH3. It is a naturally occurring substance found in various plant species, particularly those referred to as wintergreens. Plants that produce methyl salicylate synthesize this organic ester, which is a combination of an organic acid and an alcohol, likely as a defense mechanism against herbivores. Beyond its toxic properties, methyl salicylate may serve as a chemical signal or pheromone to alert neighboring plants to the presence of pathogens, such as the tobacco mosaic virus. When plants are infested with herbivorous insects, the release of methyl salicylate can attract beneficial predatory insects that help eliminate the herbivores. While many plants produce this compound in trace amounts, certain species produce it in detectable quantities, such as: Most members of the family Pyrolaceae, especially those in the genus Pyrola. Some species within the genus Gaultheria of the family Ericaceae. Certain species of the genus Betula in the family Betulaceae, particularly those in the subgenus Betulenta. Methyl salicylate can be synthesized by esterifying salicylic acid with methanol. Historically, it was distilled from the twigs of Sweet Birch (Betula lenta) and Eastern Teaberry (Gaultheria procumbens), but modern production is primarily synthetic. This compound has several applications. It is commonly used as a rubefacient in deep-heating liniments to relieve muscle pain. In small concentrations (no more than 0.04%), it is used as a flavoring agent. It also serves as a fragrance in various products and as an odor-masking agent for certain organophosphate pesticides. However, excessive application can lead to adverse effects, including stomach and kidney damage. Methyl salicylate is also of interest in the study of orchid bees, as it attracts males of various species. These bees collect the compound, likely to synthesize their own pheromones. Researchers often use methyl salicylate as bait to study and collect these bees. Additionally, it has a unique ability to clear pigments from plant or animal tissue samples, making it valuable in microscopy and immunohistochemistry when excess pigmentation obscures structural details. This clearing process is rapid but requires prior dehydration of the tissue in alcohol. Methyl salicylate can also function as a transfer agent to manually replicate images onto surfaces. Despite its utility, methyl salicylate is highly toxic in its pure form, particularly when ingested. The lowest reported lethal dose in adult humans is 101 mg per kilogram of body weight. In small children, as little as 4 mL can be fatal. A tragic example of its toxicity occurred on April 3, 2007, when a 17-year-old cross-country runner from Notre Dame Academy in Staten Island died after her body absorbed excessive amounts of methyl salicylate from overuse of topical muscle-pain relief products.
